title: Toby's Perfect Skip
markdown:
Toby the otter liked things just so. Fur smooth, as if polished. Outside the burrow, river stones lined by size and colour. His favourite quiet job was timing how long a shiny pebble took to sink. Drip, plop, tick-tock, counted in his head.

Today the job needed more than a quiet stream. Village playground: usually squeaks and splashes. Toby had a small waterproof notebook he had made himself and a pointy reed for a pencil. A serious sparkle in the otter eyes. Mission: the Perfect Skip. The exact best way to make a stone jump a puddle.

He found a flat cool stone, wiggled whiskers, puffed his chest, tossed it over a wide inviting puddle. Splash. A number in the book. Another. Splash. Another number. If he knew the precise best skip, he felt, the rest of the playground would make sense. The key to the most fun.

Ivy the wren, sunshine and giggles, fluttered down, tiny feet silent. “What are you doing? A lovely day to chase through tall grass. Tag to the oak.”

He did not look up. “The very best way to skip. Important work. I need to understand.” Another timed splash. “Slower. The air pushed it differently.”

She tilted her head. “Doesn’t it just feel nice? Without the numbers?” Wings, a little dance.

Toby frowned, a wrinkle. “Feeling good is different for everyone. Numbers stay true. They don’t change their minds.” Charts appeared: How Skips Fly Over Water. The Science of Splash Times. Pride, warm, spread. This was not only a game.

Other animals noticed. Lowenna Bear, who usually tumbled with a happy roar, peeked at the charts. “Scribbles? Secret messages for the ants?”

He puffed and explained the quest, every try written down. Lowenna, curious about a “best” skip, tossed stones, got wet paws, looked puzzled. Squirrels chattered from the trees. Rabbits twitched, wondering at the fuss.

The special sport grew. Animals gathered not to play their usual lively games but to watch him measure. They tried skips, peeked at the book, hoped to beat recorded times. Who had the best number became the only conversation by the puddle. Toby stood with the notebook feeling like an important scientist of skips. Days on, he noticed the laughter quieter, the games more like each animal playing alone. Surrounded, a hollow loneliness settled in his chest that he did not write down, because it would not fit on a chart.

One afternoon, announcing a new record for most splashes in a row, the sky went grumpy purple. Air heavy. A gust smelling of damp earth and far-off rain snatched the notebook. Pages fluttered like confused brown butterflies. A crackle: the measuring stick tore free and tumbled into the muddiest stream. Another gust landed the book in a big muddy puddle.

He watched, fur prickling. Charts, stick, organized notes — swallowed. Whiskers drooped. The playground felt grey and empty.

He sat by the puddle, soggy unreadable paper cool and pulpy. Purpose, pride, project — washed. As if the joy had been blown out.

“Toby? Are you okay?” Ivy, sparkle a little dimmed. Beside her Mrs. Flint, kind badger from the village shop, warm worried eyes.

He shook his head. No words.

Mrs. Flint sat, sturdy. “Your numbers have gone on an adventure.”

Ivy nudged his paw. “It isn’t about the numbers. Butterflies in the meadow. Hide-and-seek behind the mossy oak. That was fun too. No measuring.”

A flicker: unexpected chase, secret hiding, shared giggles. He had been so busy being best at skipping he had forgotten how to play.

Next morning the sun came out shy, then gold. Puddles like tiny mirrors. Toby walked toward a tentative gathering without notebook or stick, Ivy and Mrs. Flint beside him.

“I think I made a mistake. Being the best at skipping isn’t as fun as playing with friends. I missed the fun while I was measuring.”

Ivy’s wings beat a joyful rhythm. Mrs. Flint’s whiskers twitched. “Wise. True fun is better shared.”

They declared Community Skip Day. Everyone, big or small, skipped their best, and Toby helped them time it together: One, two, three, SKIP! Cheers not for fastest but for a stone dancing. Lowenna did a wobbly enthusiastic skip, a huge glorious splash; everyone roared. A little rabbit who had never managed a good skip produced a decent hop; claps and stomps. Toby laughed, a real one, fizzy in the chest.

The best times were not numbers that could wash away. They were gasps, delight, friendship across water. The notebook waited at home for a different kind of entry: games played, not times recorded. He joined Ivy in a chase, fur lighter, heart full. The playground buzzed with the happy chaos of playing together.

He logged splash-charts / wind-and-puddle / one-two-three-SKIP in a dry page later, left the reed pencil by the burrow stones where stones still stood in size order, and let Lowenna keep the wettest paws as a prize nobody had measured. Mrs. Flint went back to the shop with a smile that did not need a chart. The stream, which had swallowed a stick, kept being a stream, and Toby skipped without writing it down, which felt, for once, like the only correct measurement.
